Vignette:
A 31-year-old woman comes to the office because of a 6-month history of nipple discharge. She
has noticed that her breasts are tender and both nipples produce milky discharge on applying
mild pressure. She has not noted any bloody or clear nipple discharge, breast lumps, or skin
changes. She also states she has not had a menstrual period for 6 months, and her periods had
been irregular for 8 months before they stopped altogether. Prior to her menstrual irregularities,
her menses occurred at a normal frequency and duration. She is sexually active with a single
partner and is trying to conceive.

Review of Systems:
General: Gradually increasing lethargy over the past 2 months. 3 kg unintentional weight gain in
the past 6 months.

Skin: No rash or history of excessive facial hair or acne.

HEENT: No rhinorrhea, tinnitus, vertigo, or change in hearing.

Pulmonary: Noncontributory

Cardiovascular: Noncontributory

Gastrointestinal: Noncontributory

Genitourinary: Noncontributory

Gynecologic: Decreased libido. Vaginal dryness during sexual intercourse. She has been trying
to conceive for the last 2 years. One full-term, uncomplicated pregnancy 5 years ago.

Musculoskeletal: Noncontributory

Neurologic: 6-month history of dull frontal and occasionally retro-orbital headaches that are
increasing in frequency and that now occur almost daily and affect her work performance. There
are no associated neurologic symptoms, including disturbances of vision, strength, balance, or
gait. She denies nausea, photophobia, or phonophobia. Until 1 month ago, the headaches
would resolve completely with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs, but for the last month taking
simple analgesia does not suffice. She denies history of headaches prior to 6 months ago.

Psychiatric: She is mildly depressed recently, which she attributes to the frequent headaches.
No suicidal ideation.

Past Medical History:
Medical history: She had mild asthma in childhood, which she outgrew. She has a 5-year-old
son after an uncomplicated pregnancy with spontaneous vertex delivery at 40 weeks.

Surgical history: No previous operations.

Medications: Acetaminophen 1 g daily as needed; ibuprofen 400 mg daily as needed. Ibuprofen
recently increased to as much as 400 to 600 mg twice daily.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Family history: Her father had a stroke in his 80s; mother had osteoporosis.

Social history: She eats a healthy balanced diet. She does not exercise regularly. She is
nonsmoker and drinks alcohol very occasionally. She works as a primary school teacher. Her
last travel outside the country was to Italy 8 months ago.

Physical Examination:
General appearance: Comfortable-appearing female who generally looks well and appears her
stated age.

Vital signs:
BMI: 22 kg/m2
Temperature: 36.6° C
Pulse: 80 beats/minute and regular
Respirations: 18/min
BP: 135/74 mm Hg

Skin: Normal color, no rash, hirsutism, or acne.

HEENT: Pupils equal and reactive to light and accommodation. Normal visual fields to
confrontation. Visual acuity 20/20 in both eyes. Fundi normal bilaterally. No thyroid enlargement
or nodules.

Pulmonary: Equal air entry and chest is clear on auscultation. No crackles or wheezes.

Cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm with normal heart sounds. No murmurs. Normal
peripheral pulses and capillary refill.

GYN: No breast masses or skin changes. No axillary lymphadenopathy. Mild diffuse breast
tenderness on palpation. Milky nipple discharge elicited bilaterally with pressure around areolae.

Gastrointestinal: Abdomen soft, nontender, and nondistended. No organomegaly, and bowel
sounds are normal.

Genitourinary: Unremarkable

Musculoskeletal: Unremarkable

Neurologic: Normal and symmetric motor strength and reflexes on extremities. Sensation
grossly intact to light touch. Cranial nerves 2 through 12 intact. Gait and balance normal.

Mental status: Alert, oriented to person, place, and time. Affect seems slightly depressed.

Test Results:
Results of appropriate testing return and show the following (SI units are in parentheses):

Serum:
Test (units)
Result
Prolactin
500 µg/L
TSH
2.1 microIU/ml

Urine pregnancy test: Negative
MRI brain with contrast: Slightly enlarged sella turcica, sellar mass measuring 1.1 cm x 1.6 cm x
2.1 cm, no optic chiasm compression, no hydrocephalus
winner_protocol:
Age: 31
Sex: Female
Complaint: 6-month history of bilateral milky nipple discharge with breast tenderness, associated with 6 months of amenorrhea (preceded by 8 months of irregular menses), decreased libido, vaginal dryness, infertility, progressive lethargy, weight gain, and worsening daily frontal/retro-orbital headaches no longer relieved by NSAIDs.

Analysis: The combination of bilateral galactorrhea, secondary amenorrhea, decreased libido, and vaginal dryness (signs of hypoestrogenism from hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis suppression) strongly suggests hyperprolactinemia. This is confirmed by a markedly elevated serum prolactin of 500 µg/L, a level far in excess of what is typically seen with medication-induced or physiologic causes and highly suggestive of a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma). A normal TSH (2.1 microIU/mL) argues against primary hypothyroidism as a cause of secondary hyperprolactinemia. A negative urine pregnancy test excludes pregnancy as the cause of amenorrhea and galactorrhea. MRI brain with contrast confirms a sellar mass measuring 1.1 x 1.6 x 2.1 cm, consistent with a macroadenoma (greater than 1 cm), correlating with and explaining her markedly elevated prolactin. Her 6-month history of progressively worsening frontal and retro-orbital headaches, now refractory to simple analgesia, is consistent with mass effect/dural stretch from the enlarging pituitary lesion, though the MRI shows no optic chiasm compression or hydrocephalus, and her visual fields and acuity are normal, arguing against acute visual threat at this time. Fatigue, weight gain, and mild depressed mood may reflect the chronic hormonal disturbance and/or the impact of chronic headache on her wellbeing; however, other pituitary hormone axes (e.g., cortisol, thyroid function beyond TSH, growth hormone) have not yet been assessed and should be evaluated given the size of the mass and its potential to compress normal pituitary tissue, causing hypopituitarism.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Formal visual field testing by perimetry to definitively exclude any subtle chiasmal compression; full anterior pituitary hormone panel (free T4, morning cortisol or ACTH stimulation test, IGF-1, LH/FSH, estradiol) to assess for hypopituitarism from mass effect; referral to endocrinology and neurosurgery for further evaluation and monitoring.

Conclusion: Macroprolactinoma (pituitary macroadenoma with markedly elevated prolactin) causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (secondary amenorrhea, galactorrhea, infertility, decreased libido, vaginal dryness) and progressive headache, without current evidence of optic chiasm compression or hydrocephalus on MRI.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology

Recommendations: Refer promptly to endocrinology for initiation of dopamine agonist therapy (e.g., cabergoline, preferred first-line agent), which is highly effective at normalizing prolactin, shrinking the tumor, and restoring menses and fertility in most patients with prolactinomas. Obtain a complete pituitary hormone panel and formal visual field testing as above. Refer to neurosurgery for baseline evaluation given the macroadenoma size, even though surgery is not the first-line treatment for prolactinomas. Advise the patient that fertility may be restored with successful prolactin normalization, but that she should use non-hormonal contraception until pregnancy is desired and coordinate closely with endocrinology, since pregnancy can cause further tumor growth requiring monitoring. Address her worsening headaches with follow-up MRI surveillance and reassess if her headache pattern changes; discontinue excessive ibuprofen use given her recent escalation, as medication-overuse headache is a possible contributor, and provide safer, monitored pain management. Advise her to seek immediate emergency care if she develops sudden severe headache, new visual loss or diplopia, or altered mental status, which could indicate pituitary apoplexy.

Notes: Although visual fields were grossly normal on confrontation testing and MRI shows no chiasm compression, formal perimetry is recommended given the size of the macroadenoma and her worsening headaches, to detect early subclinical involvement.

Vignette:
A 44-year-old woman with known Addison disease on chronic hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement presents with 3 days of progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain following a viral gastroenteritis illness. She has been unable to keep her oral medications down for 2 days. On examination, she is lethargic and appears critically ill with notable hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa, palmar creases, and surgical scars. Vital signs: T 37.8C, HR 118, RR 22, BP 72/38 (unresponsive to 2L IV normal saline), SpO2 95%. Skin turgor is markedly decreased. Labs: sodium 118 mEq/L, potassium 6.4 mEq/L, glucose 52 mg/dL, BUN 48 mg/dL, creatinine 2.1 mg/dL, random cortisol 1.2 mcg/dL. ECG shows peaked T waves and prolonged PR interval. IV stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg is administered immediately.
winner_protocol:
Age: 44
Sex: Female
Complaint: 3 days of progressive nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain following a viral gastroenteritis illness, with inability to keep oral medications down for 2 days, in a patient with known Addison disease on chronic hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone replacement.

Analysis: This patient has known primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) and has been unable to take her oral glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement for 2 days during an intercurrent viral gastroenteritis illness, a classic precipitant of adrenal crisis due to inability to mount the normal stress-dose cortisol response and interrupted maintenance therapy. She now presents critically ill: lethargic, with severe hypotension (BP 72/38) refractory to 2 liters of IV normal saline, tachycardic (HR 118), and with markedly decreased skin turgor consistent with severe volume depletion. Hyperpigmentation of the oral mucosa, palmar creases, and surgical scars confirms chronic primary adrenal insufficiency (from elevated ACTH). Laboratory findings are diagnostic of adrenal crisis: severe hyponatremia (Na 118), hyperkalemia (K 6.4) with ECG changes (peaked T waves, prolonged PR interval) indicating cardiac toxicity from hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia (glucose 52), and an inappropriately low random cortisol (1.2 mcg/dL) in the setting of critical illness, where cortisol should be markedly elevated. Acute kidney injury (BUN 48, creatinine 2.1) is present, likely from a combination of severe volume depletion and the hemodynamic effects of the crisis. This constitutes a life-threatening adrenal (Addisonian) crisis requiring immediate glucocorticoid replacement, which has appropriately already been initiated with IV stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac monitoring given hyperkalemia with ECG changes; repeat serum electrolytes, glucose, and renal function to guide ongoing fluid and electrolyte correction; blood and stool studies to identify the underlying gastroenteritis pathogen if clinically indicated; ongoing ECG monitoring for resolution of hyperkalemic changes.

Conclusion: Acute adrenal (Addisonian) crisis precipitated by viral gastroenteritis with inability to tolerate oral glucocorticoid/mineralocorticoid replacement, presenting with refractory hypotension, severe hyponatremia, hyperkalemia with cardiac toxicity, and hypoglycemia.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology

Recommendations: This is a medical emergency requiring immediate ICU-level care. Continue and escalate IV stress-dose hydrocortisone (100 mg IV bolus already given, followed by continuous infusion or repeated dosing every 6-8 hours) which will also provide sufficient mineralocorticoid activity at high doses, obviating urgent need for separate fludrocortisone until oral intake resumes. Aggressively continue IV isotonic fluid resuscitation (normal saline) to correct hypotension and volume depletion, with close monitoring given her cardiac risk from hyperkalemia. Administer IV dextrose to correct hypoglycemia. Treat hyperkalemia with ECG changes emergently per standard protocol (calcium gluconate for cardiac membrane stabilization, insulin with dextrose and/or beta-agonist to shift potassium intracellularly, and consider potassium-lowering measures), given the peaked T waves and prolonged PR interval indicating impending arrhythmia risk. Correct hyponatremia cautiously and gradually to avoid osmotic demyelination, guided by frequent electrolyte monitoring. Identify and treat the underlying trigger (viral gastroenteritis) with supportive antiemetic therapy once she can tolerate oral or IV antiemetics. Once stabilized and tolerating oral intake, transition back to her home oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone regimen with a tapering stress-dose schedule. Educate the patient and caregivers on sick-day rules for adrenal insufficiency (doubling/tripling oral glucocorticoid dose during illness, and the need for injectable emergency hydrocortisone when oral intake is not tolerated) to prevent recurrence.

Notes: This event highlights a gap in sick-day management education; the patient should be provided with an emergency injectable hydrocortisone kit and clear instructions for future illnesses where oral medications cannot be tolerated.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) presents with rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of his right lower leg that began 2 days ago after a minor abrasion he sustained while gardening. Despite oral cephalexin started by his PCP yesterday, the erythema has expanded dramatically. On examination, he appears toxic and diaphoretic. Vital signs: T 39.8C, HR 128, RR 24, BP 92/56, SpO2 95%. The right leg demonstrates tense, dusky erythema extending from the ankle to the knee with areas of purplish discoloration and hemorrhagic bullae. Crepitus is palpable along the anterior shin. Pain is severe and extends beyond the visible margins of erythema. Labs: WBC 28,200/mcL, glucose 428 mg/dL, sodium 131 mEq/L, creatinine 2.4 mg/dL, CRP 32 mg/dL, lactate 4.6 mmol/L. LRINEC score is 10. CT of the leg shows extensive gas tracking along the fascial planes.
winner_protocol:
Age: 55
Sex: Male
Complaint: Rapidly worsening pain, swelling, and redness of the right lower leg over 2 days following a minor gardening abrasion, progressing despite oral antibiotics started the prior day.

Analysis: This presentation is highly concerning for necrotizing fasciitis, a surgical emergency. Key alarming features include rapid progression of erythema despite appropriate oral antibiotic coverage (cephalexin), pain that extends beyond the visible margins of erythema (a hallmark of necrotizing soft tissue infection, reflecting deep fascial involvement out of proportion to skin findings), tense dusky erythema with purplish discoloration and hemorrhagic bullae (signs of skin/soft tissue ischemia and necrosis), and palpable crepitus (indicating gas-forming organisms within the tissue planes). He is systemically toxic with fever (39.8C), tachycardia (128), hypotension (92/56), and diaphoresis, indicating septic shock. His poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) is a major risk factor for necrotizing fasciitis and impairs immune response. Laboratory findings support this: marked leukocytosis (28,200), significant hyperglycemia (428), hyponatremia (131), acute kidney injury (creatinine 2.4), elevated CRP, and an elevated lactate (4.6) indicating tissue hypoperfusion/ischemia. His LRINEC (Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis) score of 10 is in the high-risk category (score ≥8 strongly predictive of necrotizing fasciitis). CT imaging confirming gas tracking along fascial planes provides definitive radiographic support for the diagnosis. This constitutes a limb- and life-threatening surgical emergency requiring immediate operative intervention; imaging should not delay surgery once clinical suspicion is high.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures and wound/tissue cultures (ideally obtained intraoperatively) to guide antibiotic therapy; continued laboratory monitoring (lactate, renal function, coagulation studies, electrolytes) to guide resuscitation; the CT already obtained has confirmed fascial gas and should not delay surgical intervention.

Conclusion: Necrotizing fasciitis of the right lower leg with septic shock in a patient with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, confirmed by clinical findings (pain out of proportion, hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus), a high LRINEC score, and CT evidence of fascial gas; this is a surgical and medical emergency.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: General Surgery

Recommendations: Emergent surgical consultation for immediate operative debridement is the definitive and most time-critical intervention; do not delay surgery for further imaging or stabilization beyond initial resuscitation. Initiate broad-spectrum empiric IV antibiotics immediately, covering gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic organisms, and including an agent with antitoxin activity against toxin-producing streptococci/staphylococci (e.g., a carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin, plus clindamycin for antitoxin effect). Begin aggressive IV fluid resuscitation and hemodynamic support for septic shock, with vasopressors if hypotension persists despite fluids, and ICU-level monitoring. Correct severe hyperglycemia with an insulin infusion given the markedly elevated glucose (428) and its role in impairing host defense. Closely monitor renal function, electrolytes, and lactate clearance to guide ongoing resuscitation. Anticipate need for repeat surgical debridement(s), and involve infectious disease and, if diabetes control is markedly deranged (as here), endocrinology for glycemic management. Provide analgesia and continuous vital sign monitoring throughout.

Notes: Time to surgical debridement is the single most important determinant of outcome in necrotizing fasciitis; any delay significantly increases mortality risk. His severely uncontrolled diabetes (HbA1c 11.2%) will require ongoing intensive glycemic management as part of his overall care.

Vignette:
A 20-year-old male college athlete presents with itchy, peeling skin between his toes bilaterally for the past 2 weeks. He plays on the soccer team and uses communal showers at the athletic facility daily. He denies pain, swelling, or spreading beyond the interdigital spaces. He has no history of diabetes or immunosuppression. On examination, there is maceration and peeling of the skin in the third and fourth interdigital web spaces of both feet. Mild erythema is present. There are no vesicles, bullae, or fissures extending to the soles. Toenails appear normal.
winner_protocol:
Age: 20
Sex: Male
Complaint: Itchy, peeling skin between the toes bilaterally for 2 weeks.

Analysis: The presentation of bilateral interdigital maceration, peeling, and mild erythema confined to the third and fourth toe web spaces, with pruritus, in a young athlete who uses communal showers daily, is classic for interdigital tinea pedis (athlete's foot), a dermatophyte infection. Communal shower and locker room exposure is a well-established risk factor for dermatophyte transmission. The absence of pain, spreading beyond the web spaces, vesicles, bullae, or fissures extending to the soles argues against a more extensive or complicated presentation (such as moccasin-type tinea pedis or bullous tinea), and there is no diabetes or immunosuppression that would raise concern for a more serious or complicated skin/soft tissue infection. Normal toenails make concurrent onychomycosis unlikely at this time. The clinical picture does not suggest bacterial cellulitis (no spreading erythema, warmth, or systemic symptoms) or erythrasma (which typically has a different distribution and coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp), making tinea pedis the most likely diagnosis based on history and examination alone.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for typical presentation; if diagnosis were uncertain or the condition failed to respond to empiric antifungal therapy, a potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of skin scrapings could be performed to confirm dermatophyte infection.

Conclusion: Interdigital tinea pedis (athlete's foot), uncomplicated, likely acquired through communal shower exposure.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: Dermatology

Recommendations: Recommend a topical antifungal agent (e.g., terbinafine, clotrimazole, or miconazole cream) applied to the affected web spaces twice daily for 2-4 weeks, continuing for at least 1 week after visible resolution to reduce recurrence. Advise keeping the feet clean and thoroughly dried, especially between the toes, after showering; use of moisture-wicking socks and breathable footwear; and applying antifungal or drying powder in shoes to reduce moisture. Recommend wearing shower sandals/flip-flops in communal shower and locker room facilities to reduce reinfection and transmission to others. If symptoms do not improve after 2-4 weeks of consistent topical therapy, or if the infection spreads, involves the nails, or recurs frequently, follow-up should be arranged to consider an oral antifungal agent or to reconsider the diagnosis.

Age: 14
Sex: Male
Complaint: Nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea (6 nonbloody, moderate-volume stools per day) with mild abdominal cramps and low-grade fever, beginning 18 hours after eating undercooked chicken at a picnic.

Analysis: The temporal relationship between ingestion of undercooked chicken and onset of gastrointestinal symptoms approximately 18 hours later, with nonbloody diarrhea, cramping, low-grade fever, and vomiting, is characteristic of foodborne bacterial gastroenteritis, with Salmonella and Campylobacter being the most likely pathogens given the undercooked poultry exposure (these are classically associated with poultry and typically have an incubation period in this range). Examination findings of mild tachycardia (HR 105) with normal blood pressure, low-grade fever (100.1°F), mild diffuse abdominal tenderness, and increased bowel sounds are consistent with mild-to-moderate gastroenteritis without evidence of severe dehydration, peritoneal signs, or systemic toxicity. The absence of bloody stools is reassuring against more invasive or severe bacterial colitis (e.g., Shiga toxin-producing E. coli) or an inflammatory process, though bacterial pathogens such as Salmonella and Campylobacter can occasionally present without visible blood as well. He remains able to tolerate oral fluids, which is a favorable prognostic sign and supports outpatient management with oral rehydration rather than need for IV fluids or hospitalization at this time.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Stool studies (culture, and if indicated, stool for ova and parasites or PCR panel) are not mandatory for a mild, self-limited presentation but may be considered if symptoms worsen, persist beyond several days, or if public health reporting is relevant given probable foodborne source; routine electrolyte testing is not necessary given he is tolerating oral fluids and has stable vital signs, but should be considered if dehydration develops.

Conclusion: Acute foodborne bacterial gastroenteritis, most likely due to Salmonella or Campylobacter given the undercooked poultry exposure and incubation period, currently mild with adequate oral tolerance and no signs of severe dehydration or complication.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

winner_protocol:
Age: 28
Sex: Female
Complaint: 9-month history of chronic watery diarrhea, bloating, and 12-pound unintentional weight loss, with associated fatigue, occasional mouth sores, and iron deficiency anemia poorly responsive to oral iron.

Analysis: This chronic history of watery diarrhea, bloating, weight loss, fatigue, and mouth sores (aphthous stomatitis), combined with iron deficiency anemia refractory to oral supplementation, strongly suggests a malabsorptive process. The laboratory profile is highly supportive of celiac disease: microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.2, MCV 72) with very low ferritin (8 ng/mL) reflecting true iron deficiency, low vitamin D (15 ng/mL) indicating fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption, and a markedly elevated tissue transglutaminase IgA antibody (98 units, nearly 5-fold above the upper limit of normal) with a normal total IgA level (excluding IgA deficiency, which could otherwise cause a false-negative tTG-IgA result). This serologic pattern is highly sensitive and specific for celiac disease. Her low BMI (18.5) and diffuse abdominal tenderness are consistent with chronic malabsorption and weight loss. The absence of skin rash argues against dermatitis herpetiformis at this time, though this remains a related consideration. Other causes of chronic diarrhea (infectious, inflammatory bowel disease, thyroid dysfunction) are less well supported by this specific antibody and nutritional deficiency pattern, and the elevated tTG-IgA in the context of these classic malabsorptive features makes celiac disease the most likely unifying diagnosis; endoscopic biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis histologically before committing to lifelong dietary therapy.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsies (multiple, from the duodenal bulb and distal duodenum) to confirm villous atrophy and establish a definitive histologic diagnosis of celiac disease, ideally performed before initiating a gluten-free diet; bone density (DEXA) scan given chronicity and malabsorption; additional nutritional labs (vitamin B12, folate, calcium, zinc) to assess for further deficiencies; referral to gastroenterology for endoscopy and ongoing management.

Conclusion: Clinical and serologic picture strongly consistent with celiac disease (elevated tTG-IgA with normal total IgA, chronic diarrhea, weight loss, iron deficiency anemia, and vitamin D deficiency), pending confirmatory duodenal biopsy.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Gastroenterology

Recommendations: Refer to gastroenterology for upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy to confirm the diagnosis before starting a gluten-free diet, as biopsy accuracy is reduced once gluten is removed from the diet. Advise the patient to continue a normal gluten-containing diet until biopsy is completed. Once celiac disease is confirmed, initiate a strict lifelong gluten-free diet with dietitian referral for education and support. Treat iron deficiency anemia; if oral iron continues to be poorly tolerated or absorbed due to ongoing malabsorption, consider IV iron replacement, particularly once gluten-free diet is established and malabsorption is expected to improve. Supplement vitamin D and monitor levels, and screen for and replete other potential deficiencies (B12, folate, calcium). Arrange follow-up serologic testing (repeat tTG-IgA) and clinical reassessment several months after starting a gluten-free diet to confirm response and dietary adherence. Screen for associated autoimmune conditions (e.g., thyroid disease) given the known association with celiac disease, and consider screening first-degree relatives given the hereditary component of celiac disease.

Notes: Endoscopic biopsy should be obtained prior to gluten elimination to avoid false-negative histology; if the patient has already reduced gluten intake, this should be clarified before proceeding.

Recommendations: Refer to gastroenterology for upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsy to confirm the diagnosis before starting a gluten-free diet, as biopsy accuracy is reduced once gluten is removed from the diet. Advise the patient to continue a normal gluten-containing diet until biopsy is completed. Once celiac disease is confirmed, initiate a strict lifelong gluten-free diet with dietitian referral for education and support. Treat iron deficiency anemia; if oral iron continues to be poorly tolerated or absorbed due to ongoing malabsorption, consider IV iron replacement, particularly once gluten-free diet is established and malabsorption is expected to improve. Supplement vitamin D and monitor levels, and screen for and replete other potential deficiencies (B12, folate, calcium). Arrange follow-up serologic testing (repeat tTG-IgA) and clinical reassessment several months after starting a gluten-free diet to confirm response and dietary adherence. Screen for associated autoimmune conditions (e.g., thyroid disease) given the known association with celiac disease, and consider screening first-degree relatives given the hereditary component of celiac disease.

Notes: Endoscopic biopsy should be obtained prior to gluten elimination to avoid false-negative histology; if the patient has already reduced gluten intake, this should be clarified before proceeding.

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

[6]
tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Complaint: Episode of confusion and amnesia the night before presentation, preceded by extreme fatigue after modest wine intake, with reported tossing in bed, a lateral tongue laceration with blood in the mouth, bilateral upper extremity soreness, urinary incontinence during sleep, and prolonged sleep afterward, now with resolved confusion.

Analysis: The constellation of findings, going to bed early due to unusual fatigue, an unwitnessed nocturnal event with "tossing around in bed" observed by her husband, subsequent amnesia for the event, a lateral tongue laceration (a highly specific finding for a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, as tongue biting during seizures characteristically occurs on the lateral edge), bilateral upper extremity soreness (consistent with tonic-clonic muscle contraction), urinary incontinence, and an abnormally prolonged postictal sleep period, is classic for an unwitnessed nocturnal generalized tonic-clonic seizure with a postictal state, rather than simple alcohol-related sedation from only 2-3 glasses of wine. Her basic metabolic panel is essentially unremarkable (mild hyponatremia at 133, not low enough to typically provoke seizure), glucose is normal, liver enzymes are normal, and her alcohol level at the time of testing is low (10 mg/dL), making a purely toxic/metabolic or alcohol withdrawal cause unlikely to fully explain a first seizure. ECG and urine toxicology are unremarkable, and EEG shows no epileptiform discharges (though a normal interictal EEG does not exclude epilepsy or a seizure having occurred). Critically, CT imaging reveals an ill-defined rounded mass adjacent to the dura of the posterior falx, and MRI was obtained for further characterization; a dural-based mass in this location is most consistent with a meningioma, a recognized structural cause of new-onset seizures in an older adult. This represents a first-ever seizure with an identified structural intracranial lesion, which substantially raises her risk of seizure recurrence and requires urgent neurological evaluation, even though she has returned to her neurological baseline (normal exam, alert and oriented, normal gait/coordination) at the time of assessment.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: MRI of the brain with and without contrast for full characterization of the dural-based mass (already noted as obtained; results should be formally reviewed for size, enhancement pattern, and any mass effect); neurosurgical and neurology consultation for further evaluation of the lesion and seizure management; continued cardiac and neurological monitoring while inpatient.

Conclusion: First-ever unwitnessed nocturnal generalized tonic-clonic seizure, now postictal and returned to neurological baseline, associated with an incidentally identified dural-based mass (likely meningioma) adjacent to the posterior falx, which is the probable structural cause.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Recommendations: Admit for further observation and inpatient neurology consultation given a first-time seizure associated with a newly identified structural brain lesion, to assess seizure recurrence risk and determine need for antiepileptic drug therapy. Obtain formal neurosurgical evaluation of the dural-based mass to characterize it (contrast-enhanced MRI, likely already obtained) and determine whether surgical resection, radiosurgery, or watchful monitoring is appropriate, as many meningiomas are managed conservatively depending on size, location, and symptoms. Provide seizure precautions and safety counseling, including driving restrictions per local regulations following a first unprovoked seizure. Address the tongue laceration with local wound care; it is superficial and unlikely to require repair. Counsel the patient and husband on recognizing further seizure activity and the importance of prompt medical attention should recurrence occur. Arrange close outpatient neurology follow-up after discharge to determine whether initiation of an antiepileptic medication is warranted given the identified structural lesion.

Notes: Although her repeat neurological examination and EEG are currently normal, the presence of a structural dural-based lesion adjacent to the falx warrants close follow-up, as this materially changes her risk of seizure recurrence compared with an idiopathic first seizure.

A 38-year-old woman presents with a 3-week history of persistent throat clearing and a mild cough that is worse when lying down at night. She reports a sensation of mucus dripping in the back of her throat. She recently had a mild cold that resolved 4 weeks ago. She denies fever, facial pain, purulent nasal discharge, wheezing, or heartburn. She is a non-smoker. On examination, the oropharynx shows a cobblestone appearance of the posterior pharyngeal wall. winner_protocol:
Age: 38
Sex: Female
Complaint: 3-week history of persistent throat clearing and mild nocturnal cough, with a sensation of mucus dripping in the back of the throat, following a mild cold that resolved 4 weeks ago.

Analysis: The presenting symptoms of chronic throat clearing, a sensation of postnasal mucus drip, and cough that worsens when lying down (consistent with secretions pooling in the pharynx in the recumbent position) occurring in the weeks following a resolved viral upper respiratory infection are classic for postinfectious postnasal drip syndrome (upper airway cough syndrome). Examination supports this: cobblestone appearance of the posterior pharyngeal wall (from chronic lymphoid hyperplasia due to repeated mucus contact) and mildly erythematous nasal mucosa with clear thin secretions. The absence of fever, facial pain, purulent nasal discharge, and lack of sinus tenderness argues against acute or subacute bacterial sinusitis. Clear lung auscultation without wheeze makes an asthma-predominant or lower airway cause less likely, and denial of heartburn makes gastroesophageal reflux a less likely primary contributor, though it remains a differential consideration for chronic cough if postnasal drip treatment fails. The temporal relationship to a preceding viral illness and the clinical findings together support postviral/postnasal drip as the most likely cause of her persistent cough and throat clearing, a common and generally self-limited to subacute cause of cough lasting 3-8 weeks.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required initially, as the diagnosis is supported by history and examination; if symptoms fail to improve with empiric therapy over several weeks, consider further evaluation including allergy testing, sinus imaging, or referral for chronic cough workup (including consideration of gastroesophageal reflux or asthma testing).

Conclusion: Postviral (postinfectious) postnasal drip syndrome causing subacute cough and throat clearing, without evidence of bacterial sinusitis, asthma, or reflux.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

Recommendations: Recommend a trial of empiric therapy for postnasal drip, such as an intranasal corticosteroid spray and/or a first-generation antihistamine (e.g., diphenhydramine or a combination antihistamine-decongestant), which are typically effective for postinfectious upper airway cough syndrome. Saline nasal irrigation may also help clear residual secretions and reduce mucosal irritation. Advise elevating the head of the bed to reduce nocturnal symptoms from secretion pooling. Reassure the patient that this is a common, self-limited process following viral illness that typically resolves over several weeks with symptomatic treatment. winner_protocol:
Age: 19
Sex: Male
Complaint: Sudden onset of sharp right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea beginning 2 hours ago while playing basketball.

Analysis: This presentation is classic for a primary spontaneous pneumothorax. The patient's body habitus, tall and thin (6'3", 145 lbs, giving a low BMI), is a well-recognized risk factor for primary spontaneous pneumothorax due to increased likelihood of subpleural bleb rupture at the lung apices related to increased transpulmonary pressure gradients in tall individuals. He has no prior lung disease, trauma, or smoking history, supporting a primary (rather than secondary) spontaneous pneumothorax. Examination confirms the diagnosis: hyperresonance to percussion and decreased breath sounds on the affected right side, consistent with air in the pleural space. He is tachycardic (HR 104) and tachypneic (RR 22) with mild hypoxemia (SpO2 93%), indicating physiologic compromise from a large pneumothorax, though he remains hemodynamically stable and able to speak in full sentences, arguing against tension physiology at this moment. Chest X-ray confirms a large right pneumothorax with approximately 60% lung collapse; the absence of mediastinal shift is reassuring against tension pneumothorax, though a large pneumothorax of this size with hypoxemia and tachycardia requires urgent intervention rather than observation alone, which would only be appropriate for a small, asymptomatic pneumothorax.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous pulse oximetry and cardiac monitoring; repeat chest X-ray after intervention to confirm lung re-expansion; equipment for chest tube thoracostomy or needle/catheter aspiration as definitive treatment.

Conclusion: Large (approximately 60%) right-sided primary spontaneous pneumothorax in a tall, thin young man, causing hypoxemia and tachycardia, without current evidence of tension physiology or mediastinal shift.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Pulmonology

Recommendations: Given the large size (60% collapse) and associated hypoxemia and tachycardia, this requires emergent intervention rather than observation; proceed with chest tube thoracostomy (tube thoracostomy) for lung re-expansion, as needle aspiration is generally reserved for smaller pneumothoraces or as a temporizing measure. Provide supplemental oxygen to help hasten resorption of pleural air and correct hypoxemia. Continuously monitor vital signs and oxygen saturation for any signs of progression to tension pneumothorax (worsening hypotension, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins), which would require immediate needle decompression. Obtain a repeat chest X-ray after chest tube placement to confirm resolution of the pneumothorax and correct tube positioning. Admit for observation until the lung has re-expanded and the chest tube can be safely removed. Counsel the patient on the significant risk of recurrence of primary spontaneous pneumothorax (roughly 30% or higher after a first episode) and discuss the option of pleurodesis or surgical intervention (e.g., video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery) especially if recurrence occurs. Advise avoidance of air travel and scuba diving until cleared by pulmonology, and avoidance of strenuous activity until full resolution and follow-up clearance.

Notes: Recurrence risk after a first spontaneous pneumothorax is substantial; the patient should be counseled on recognizing recurrent symptoms and the potential need for future surgical management (e.g., pleurodesis) after this or a subsequent episode.

A 50-year-old woman presents with a 5-day history of persistent dizziness described as a sensation of spinning. She reports the dizziness is constant rather than positional and is accompanied by an unsteady gait and difficulty walking in a straight line. She has had two episodes of nausea and vomiting. She denies hearing loss or tinnitus. Past medical history is notable for migraine headaches and hypertension. On examination, vital signs are stable. winner_protocol:
Age: 50
Sex: Female
Complaint: 5-day history of persistent, constant (non-positional) vertigo with unsteady gait, difficulty walking straight, and two episodes of nausea and vomiting.

Analysis: Several features in this presentation raise concern for a central rather than peripheral cause of vertigo. The dizziness is described as constant rather than positional or episodic, which is atypical for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) or vestibular neuritis, both of which are more commonly triggered or worsened by position changes and improve between episodes. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver is negative, arguing against BPPV. Critically, the neurological examination reveals vertical nystagmus that does not suppress with visual fixation, this pattern is a recognized red flag for a central vestibular lesion, as peripheral causes of vertigo typically produce horizontal or horizontal-torsional nystagmus that suppresses with fixation. Additionally, she has mild dysmetria on finger-to-nose testing on the right and gait ataxia with veering to the right, both localizing to cerebellar dysfunction, most consistent with a lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere or its connections. Hearing is intact bilaterally, and there is no tinnitus, making an inner ear (labyrinthine) process such as Meniere disease or labyrinthitis less likely as the sole explanation, since these typically also involve the cochlear apparatus in addition to the vestibular system. Her history of hypertension is a vascular risk factor. Taken together, this constellation, constant vertigo, central-type nystagmus, cerebellar signs (dysmetria and ataxia), and a vascular risk factor, is concerning for a posterior circulation (vertebrobasilar) stroke or other acute cerebellar process (such as cerebellar hemorrhage or a mass lesion), which constitutes a neurological emergency (a "cerebellar/posterior circulation stroke mimicking peripheral vertigo" presentation, sometimes summarized by HINTS-type red flags for central vertigo).

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Urgent MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), which is more sensitive than CT for acute posterior fossa/cerebellar ischemic stroke; if MRI is not immediately available, an urgent non-contrast CT head as an initial screen, though a normal CT does not exclude an early posterior circulation stroke; continuous vital sign and neurological monitoring; consider formal bedside oculomotor (HINTS) examination by a neurologist to further characterize central versus peripheral findings.

Conclusion: Constant vertigo with central-type nystagmus and cerebellar signs (dysmetria, gait ataxia), concerning for an acute posterior circulation (cerebellar) stroke or other central cerebellar pathology, requiring urgent neuroimaging and neurology evaluation.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Neurology

Recommendations: This patient should be referred immediately for emergent evaluation given red-flag findings for a central cause of vertigo (constant symptoms, non-fixation-suppressing vertical nystagmus, dysmetria, and gait ataxia). Obtain urgent MRI brain with DWI to evaluate for posterior circulation (cerebellar) ischemic stroke; if stroke is confirmed and within the appropriate treatment window, evaluate for thrombolysis or other acute stroke intervention per current stroke protocols. Obtain neurology consultation urgently. Maintain close neurological monitoring given the risk of cerebellar edema and potential for brainstem compression or hydrocephalus with larger cerebellar strokes, which can deteriorate rapidly and require neurosurgical intervention. Address vascular risk factors (hypertension) as part of secondary stroke prevention once the acute diagnosis is established. Do not attribute her symptoms to migraine or benign peripheral vertigo given the presence of these central examination findings, despite her history of migraine.

Notes: Although she has a history of migraine, which can occasionally cause vertigo, the presence of non-fixation-suppressing vertical nystagmus, dysmetria, and ataxia are red flags that must not be attributed to a benign peripheral or migrainous cause without urgent central-cause exclusion first.

It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.

First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. - If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Mr. A is a 24 year-old man who presents to your office for complaints of sore throat, fever, and headache. His symptoms started 2 days ago with acute onset of sore throat and fever to 102.2. He has had no cough. His physical examination is normal, except for the presence of tonsillar exudates and some tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy. winner_protocol:
Age: 24
Sex: Male
Complaint: 2-day history of acute sore throat, fever to 102.2°F, and headache, without cough.

Analysis: This patient presents with acute pharyngitis characterized by fever, sore throat, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and notably the absence of cough. Applying the Centor criteria (fever, tonsillar exudates, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, and absence of cough), he meets all four criteria for a Centor score of 4, which corresponds to a high pretest probability (approximately 50-60%) of group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis. A Centor score of 4 falls into the category where either empiric antibiotic treatment or rapid antigen/culture testing followed by treatment if positive is a reasonable management strategy, as noted in the case. The absence of cough, rhinorrhea, or other viral upper respiratory symptoms further supports a bacterial rather than viral etiology, since viral pharyngitis more commonly presents with concurrent cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. He is otherwise healthy with no drug allergies, which simplifies antibiotic selection if treatment is pursued. There is no mention of drooling, trismus, muffled voice, or asymmetric tonsillar bulging, which would raise concern for a peritonsillar abscess, and no respiratory distress or stridor to suggest airway compromise.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Rapid antigen detection test (RADT) for group A Streptococcus, with backup throat culture if the rapid test is negative and clinical suspicion remains high, to confirm the diagnosis and guide antibiotic use given a Centor score of 4 (test-and-treat approach is reasonable and helps avoid unnecessary antibiotic use).

Conclusion: Acute pharyngitis with a Centor score of 4, highly suggestive of group A streptococcal pharyngitis; confirmatory rapid strep testing (or empiric treatment) is appropriate given this high pretest probability.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

Recommendations: Perform a rapid antigen detection test for group A Streptococcus (with reflex throat culture if negative, given the high pretest probability from a Centor score of 4); alternatively, given his Centor score of 4, empiric antibiotic treatment without testing is also an acceptable strategy per Centor score guidance. If testing is positive or empiric treatment is chosen, prescribe a standard course of penicillin or amoxicillin (first-line, given no penicillin allergy), with a full 10-day course to reduce the risk of rheumatic fever and other complications; alternative agents can be used if allergy develops or is discovered. Continue supportive care with ibuprofen for fever and pain, adequate hydration, and rest. Advise the patient that he is contagious and should avoid close contact with others, particularly avoid returning to work/school, until he has completed at least 24 hours of antibiotic therapy and is afebrile. Advise him to seek prompt medical attention if he develops difficulty swallowing or breathing, drooling, inability to open his mouth fully, or worsening unilateral throat swelling, which would raise concern for peritonsillar abscess or airway compromise.

Vignette:
A 19-year-old man presents with a 5-day history of severe sore throat that has progressively worsened despite 3 days of oral amoxicillin prescribed for pharyngitis. He now reports difficulty swallowing and has been unable to eat solid food for 2 days. He describes a muffled "hot potato" voice and difficulty fully opening his mouth. He has been drooling due to pain with swallowing. He denies respiratory difficulty. Vital signs show temperature 101.4°F, heart rate 98, blood pressure 124/78. On examination, there is trismus with limited mouth opening to approximately 2 cm. Intraoral exam reveals a bulging, erythematous soft palate on the left with displacement of the left tonsil medially and inferiorly. The uvula is deviated to the right. There is tender left anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy. Lung auscultation is clear and there is no stridor.
winner_protocol:
Age: 19
Sex: Male
Complaint: 5-day history of severe sore throat progressively worsening despite 3 days of oral amoxicillin, now with odynophagia preventing solid food intake for 2 days, muffled "hot potato" voice, trismus, and drooling.

Analysis: This presentation is classic for a peritonsillar abscess. The clinical picture of worsening sore throat despite antibiotics targeted at pharyngitis, combined with the hallmark tetrad of trismus (limited mouth opening to approximately 2 cm), a muffled "hot potato" voice, drooling from inability to swallow secretions, and unilateral tonsillar findings, strongly supports this diagnosis. Examination confirms it definitively: a bulging, erythematous left soft palate with medial and inferior displacement of the left tonsil and contralateral uvular deviation (to the right) are the classic findings of a peritonsillar abscess collecting lateral to the tonsillar capsule. Tender left anterior cervical and submandibular lymphadenopathy reflects the regional inflammatory response. Fever (101.4°F) and tachycardia (HR 98) indicate an ongoing systemic infectious/inflammatory process. Importantly, he denies respiratory difficulty and has clear lung auscultation with no stridor, which is reassuring against current airway compromise, though this can evolve and requires close monitoring, as peritonsillar abscess can progress to airway obstruction or spread to deeper neck spaces (e.g., parapharyngeal space, mediastinum) if untreated. Failure to improve on oral amoxicillin for pharyngitis is consistent with progression from cellulitis to a drainable abscess collection, which will not resolve with antibiotics alone and requires drainage.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None strictly required before intervention, as this is a clinical diagnosis; needle aspiration itself is both diagnostic (confirms pus) and therapeutic. If diagnosis were uncertain or deep space extension were suspected, contrast-enhanced CT of the neck could be obtained to delineate the extent of the abscess and evaluate for parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal extension, particularly given the significant trismus limiting full oral examination.

Conclusion: Left-sided peritonsillar abscess, evidenced by trismus, muffled voice, drooling, and characteristic asymmetric tonsillar bulging with uvular deviation, progressing despite oral antibiotics for presumed pharyngitis; requires urgent drainage.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

Recommendations: Urgent otolaryngology (ENT) consultation for needle aspiration or incision and drainage of the peritonsillar abscess, which is both diagnostic and the definitive treatment. Initiate IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering typical peritonsillar abscess pathogens (group A Streptococcus, oral anaerobes, and Staphylococcus aureus), such as ampicillin-sulbactam or clindamycin, given his failure of oral amoxicillin and inability to tolerate oral intake. Provide IV fluids given his 2-day inability to eat solid food and likely reduced oral fluid intake, and adequate analgesia. Closely monitor airway status given trismus and drooling, with low threshold for airway intervention (e.g., anesthesia/ENT standby) if any signs of respiratory distress or stridor develop. Provide IV corticosteroids as adjunct therapy, which can help reduce pain, trismus, and edema. After drainage and clinical improvement, transition to oral antibiotics to complete a full course (typically 10-14 days total). Arrange close follow-up to ensure resolution and consider referral for tonsillectomy evaluation if there is a history of recurrent tonsillitis or peritonsillar abscess.

Notes: Although he currently denies respiratory difficulty and has no stridor, peritonsillar abscess can progress rapidly to airway compromise or deep neck space infection; close monitoring is essential until drainage is performed and improvement is confirmed.

Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.

Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a 1-week history of mildly itchy, erythematous patches on both hands. He recently switched to a new laundry detergent approximately two weeks ago. He denies any history of atopic dermatitis, asthma, or food allergies. On examination, there are bilateral, symmetric, well-demarcated erythematous plaques on the dorsal hands with mild scaling. The skin is intact with no cracking, vesicles, or weeping. There is no involvement of the wrists or forearms. He works as an accountant and reports no occupational chemical exposures.
winner_protocol:
Age: 30
Sex: Male
Complaint: 1-week history of mildly itchy, erythematous patches on both hands, following a recent switch to a new laundry detergent approximately two weeks ago.

Analysis: The temporal association between switching to a new laundry detergent (an item that contacts clothing and, by extension, the hands during handling and wearing) approximately two weeks before symptom onset, and the subsequent development of bilateral, symmetric, well-demarcated erythematous plaques with mild scaling on the dorsal hands, is strongly suggestive of allergic or irritant contact dermatitis. The well-demarcated, symmetric distribution limited to areas of presumed detergent contact (dorsal hands, without involvement of the wrists or forearms, which may have had less direct or prolonged contact) supports an exogenous contactant as the cause rather than an endogenous eczematous process. The absence of a personal history of atopic dermatitis, asthma, or food allergies makes an atopic dermatitis flare somewhat less likely, though it does not exclude a new presentation. He denies occupational chemical exposure, further supporting the laundry detergent as the likely culprit allergen or irritant. The skin remains intact without cracking, vesicles, or weeping, indicating a mild-to-moderate, uncomplicated presentation without secondary infection or an acute vesicular allergic reaction.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None required for this classic presentation; if the dermatitis persists or recurs despite avoidance measures, patch testing could be considered to identify a specific contact allergen.

Conclusion: Allergic or irritant contact dermatitis of the dorsal hands, most likely related to a new laundry detergent exposure.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: Dermatology

Recommendations: Advise discontinuing the new laundry detergent and returning to the previously used product, or switching to a fragrance-free, dye-free, hypoallergenic detergent, and thoroughly rewashing clothing and bedding to remove residual detergent. Recommend a low-to-mid potency topical corticosteroid cream applied to the affected areas for a short course (e.g., 1-2 weeks) to reduce inflammation and itching. Advise use of a bland emollient moisturizer to support skin barrier repair, and avoidance of further contact with the suspected irritant/allergen. Advise the patient that symptoms should improve within 1-2 weeks after eliminating the causative exposure. Advise follow-up if the rash worsens, spreads to new areas, develops vesicles or weeping (suggesting a more severe allergic reaction or superimposed infection), or fails to improve despite avoidance and topical treatment, at which point patch testing to identify a specific allergen may be warranted.

Notes: None.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
