Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

winner_protocol:
Age: 56
Sex: Male
Complaint: 6 days of non-productive cough, nasal congestion, green nasal discharge, and intermittent fevers up to 100.8F.

Analysis: The patient presents with a nearly week-long course of nasal congestion, purulent (green) nasal discharge, non-productive cough, and low-grade intermittent fever. The physical examination is essentially normal apart from rhinorrhea, with no mention of facial pain/pressure, periorbital swelling, severe headache, or signs of systemic toxicity. Viral upper respiratory infections commonly produce discolored nasal discharge as part of the natural course and do not necessarily indicate bacterial sinusitis; the duration of 6 days is at the shorter end of the typical threshold (symptoms persisting beyond 10 days without improvement, or "double worsening," are more suggestive of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis). Given the relatively short duration, absence of facial pain/pressure, absence of high fever, and an otherwise normal exam, this is most consistent with a viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold), though early bacterial rhinosinusitis remains a differential that should be reconsidered if symptoms persist or worsen. His chronic osteoarthritis of the knee is unrelated to the current presentation. No red-flag features (severe headache, visual changes, periorbital swelling, altered mental status) are present to suggest a complication.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None at this stage; the diagnosis is clinical. If symptoms persist beyond 10 days without improvement, worsen after initial improvement, or a high fever with facial pain develops, sinus imaging or ENT evaluation could be considered at that time.

Conclusion: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold) with associated nasal congestion, purulent rhinorrhea, cough, and low-grade fever; early or evolving acute bacterial rhinosinusitis cannot be entirely excluded and should be reconsidered if the course is prolonged or worsens.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: Otolaryngology (ENT)

Recommendations: Advise supportive care: rest, adequate hydration, saline nasal irrigation/sprays to help clear congestion, and over-the-counter antipyretics/analgesics (e.g., acetaminophen) for fever and discomfort as needed, noting he has no drug allergies. Decongestants or antihistamines may be used for symptomatic relief if desired. Advise that antibiotics are not indicated at this time given the short duration and absence of features suggestive of bacterial sinusitis, and that green nasal discharge alone does not indicate a bacterial infection. Instruct the patient to seek medical follow-up if symptoms persist beyond 10 days without improvement, worsen after initial improvement ("double worsening"), or if he develops high fever, significant facial pain/pressure, periorbital swelling, or severe headache, as these would warrant evaluation for bacterial rhinosinusitis or another complication.

Vignette:
A 65-year-old woman presents with unilateral leg pain and swelling of 5 days' duration. There is a history of hypertension, mild CHF, and recent hospitalization for pneumonia. She had been recuperating at home but on beginning to mobilize and walk, the right leg became painful, tender, and swollen. On examination, the right calf is 4 cm greater in circumference than the left when measured 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity. Superficial veins in the leg are more dilated on the right foot and the right leg is slightly redder than the left. There is some tenderness on palpation in the popliteal fossa behind the knee.
winner_protocol:
Age: 65
Sex: Female
Complaint: 5-day history of unilateral (right) leg pain and swelling, developing during remobilization after a recent hospitalization for pneumonia.

Analysis: This presentation carries a high pretest probability for deep vein thrombosis (DVT). Key risk factors are present: recent hospitalization and a period of immobility (recuperating from pneumonia), older age, and a history of mild CHF, all of which promote venous stasis and hypercoagulability (Virchow triad). The onset of pain, tenderness, and swelling coinciding with resumption of walking after a period of bed rest is a classic scenario for DVT presenting on remobilization. Examination findings support this: a measurable calf circumference difference (right calf 4 cm greater than left), dilated superficial veins on the affected side, mild erythema, and tenderness in the popliteal fossa, all recognized clinical signs associated with DVT (consistent with a high Wells score). Differential considerations include cellulitis, which can cause redness and swelling but typically presents with more diffuse warmth/erythema and systemic signs of infection rather than the focal popliteal tenderness and asymmetric calf girth described; a ruptured Baker cyst can mimic DVT with posterior knee pain and calf swelling and should remain in the differential; muscle strain is possible but less likely given the recent immobilization risk factor and the specific findings. Given her CHF history, bilateral chronic venous insufficiency/edema is possible but does not explain an acute unilateral asymmetric change over 5 days.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Doppler (compression) ultrasound of the right lower extremity to confirm or exclude DVT; D-dimer may be considered as an adjunct though less useful given her high pretest probability; basic labs (CBC, renal function, coagulation studies) in anticipation of anticoagulation therapy if DVT is confirmed.

Conclusion: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of acute right lower extremity deep vein thrombosis, precipitated by recent immobilization during hospitalization for pneumonia; confirmatory ultrasound imaging is required.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Cardiology

Recommendations: Arrange urgent Doppler ultrasound of the right leg to confirm the diagnosis of DVT. Pending confirmation, consider empiric anticoagulation if clinical suspicion is high and imaging cannot be obtained immediately, weighing bleeding risk. If DVT is confirmed, initiate therapeutic anticoagulation (e.g., low molecular weight heparin or a direct oral anticoagulant) per standard protocols, taking her CHF and renal function into account when selecting the agent and dose. Advise leg elevation and avoid vigorous massage of the affected limb. Educate the patient on warning signs of pulmonary embolism (sudden shortness of breath, chest pain, hemoptysis, tachycardia) and instruct her to seek emergency care immediately if these occur, given the risk of clot embolization. Arrange follow-up to monitor anticoagulation therapy and reassess for resolution of symptoms. Address her CHF and mobility plan to reduce future thromboembolic risk, including consideration of compression stockings and early mobilization protocols after future hospitalizations.

Notes: Pulmonary embolism must be considered as a possible complication and excluded clinically if she develops respiratory symptoms; this protocol addresses the leg findings, but any new cardiopulmonary symptoms would require immediate emergency evaluation.

Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 60-year-old woman presents with a 3-day history of a painful, burning, vesicular rash on the left side of her forehead extending to the tip of her nose. She initially experienced a prodrome of tingling and deep aching pain over the left forehead for 2 days before the rash appeared. She now reports left eye redness, tearing, photophobia, and a gritty foreign body sensation. She has a history of well-controlled hypertension and had chickenpox as a child. She has not received the herpes zoster vaccine. On examination, temperature is 99.4°F. There are grouped vesicles on an erythematous base distributed along the left V1 (ophthalmic) division of the trigeminal nerve, involving the forehead, upper eyelid, and the tip of the nose (positive Hutchinson sign). The left eye shows conjunctival injection, mild periorbital edema, and a mildly hazy cornea. Visual acuity is 20/40 on the left (baseline 20/25) and 20/25 on the right. Intraocular pressure is 14 mmHg bilaterally. The right side of the face is entirely clear.
winner_protocol:
Age: 60
Sex: Female
Complaint: 3-day painful, burning vesicular rash on the left forehead extending to the tip of the nose, preceded by a 2-day prodrome of tingling/aching pain, now with left eye redness, tearing, photophobia, and a gritty foreign-body sensation.

Analysis: The dermatomal distribution of grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the left V1 (ophthalmic) division of the trigeminal nerve, preceded by a prodrome of pain/tingling, is diagnostic of herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Involvement of the tip of the nose (positive Hutchinson sign, reflecting nasociliary nerve involvement) is a well-established clinical predictor of ocular involvement, which is corroborated here by the presence of conjunctival injection, periorbital edema, a hazy cornea, and decreased visual acuity (20/40 from a baseline of 20/25) in the affected eye, all suggestive of keratitis and possible uveitis. The strictly unilateral distribution with the contralateral face completely clear supports a dermatomal viral reactivation process rather than a bilateral or non-dermatomal dermatitis. Her age (over 50), history of childhood chickenpox (varicella), and lack of zoster vaccination are recognized risk factors for herpes zoster reactivation. Intraocular pressure is currently normal bilaterally (14 mmHg), which is reassuring against acute angle closure or significant secondary glaucoma at this time, but ongoing ocular inflammation can still threaten vision if untreated. This requires urgent combined antiviral and ophthalmologic management due to the risk of corneal scarring, uveitis, and vision loss.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Slit-lamp examination with fluorescein staining by ophthalmology to assess corneal involvement (dendritic or pseudodendritic keratitis), fundoscopic examination, and intraocular pressure monitoring; PCR or Tzanck smear of vesicle fluid can confirm varicella-zoster virus if diagnosis is in doubt, though this is typically a clinical diagnosis.

Conclusion: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (V1 dermatome) with a positive Hutchinson sign and clinical evidence of ocular involvement (conjunctivitis, corneal haze, and reduced visual acuity), representing a vision- and potentially globe-threatening condition requiring urgent treatment.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Ophthalmology

Recommendations: Initiate systemic antiviral therapy (e.g., oral valacyclovir or famciclovir, or intravenous acyclovir if severe) as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours of rash onset, to reduce the risk of ocular and other complications. Obtain urgent same-day ophthalmology consultation for slit-lamp evaluation given the Hutchinson sign and existing signs of keratitis/uveitis; ophthalmology will determine need for topical antivirals, cycloplegics, and/or topical corticosteroids (the latter only under specialist guidance, as they can worsen certain herpetic eye conditions if misused). Provide analgesia for the painful prodrome/rash, which can be significant, and counsel about the risk of postherpetic neuralgia. Keep the affected skin clean and avoid touching or rubbing the eye. Monitor visual acuity and intraocular pressure closely with ophthalmology follow-up. Educate the patient on warning signs of worsening ocular involvement (increasing pain, worsening vision, increased redness) requiring immediate return. Advise on the availability of the herpes zoster vaccine for prevention of future episodes once the acute illness resolves.

Notes: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus with Hutchinson sign carries a substantially increased risk of ocular complications and requires prompt, coordinated antiviral and ophthalmologic management to prevent permanent visual impairment.

Vignette: A 3-week-old male neonate is brought in by his mother who reports that the baby has been feeding poorly for the past 12 hours and seems unusually sleepy. He was born full-term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery. The mother notes the baby feels warm but did not take a temperature. On examination, the infant is lethargic with a weak cry. Vital signs: T 38.6C (rectal), HR 188, RR 52, BP 58/34. The anterior fontanelle is full and slightly bulging. The infant is hypotonic with poor suck reflex. There is no obvious rash. Skin appears mottled. WBC is 22,400/mcL with 68% neutrophils. CRP is elevated at 8.4 mg/dL. Lumbar puncture yields cloudy cerebrospinal fluid with WBC 1,200/mcL, protein 280 mg/dL, glucose 18 mg/dL.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,
- "None" is used for a field that this case clearly requires, for example no further workup is proposed although the conclusion is not yet established.
Do not fail a field merely because information that properly belongs in another field is not duplicated there.
Judge only whether the required content is present. The medical correctness of the content that is present is graded elsewhere, and so is the wording in which expectations are conveyed to the patient.

tags: ['axis:reasoning']
criterion:
Step 1:Does the Analysis field make the reasoning from the case findings to the Conclusion traceable?  The key findings that actually support the stated conclusion must be named, and the Analysis must make clear why they support that conclusion rather than merely listing case facts or restating the diagnosis. Where the protocol raises competing explanations it must say what makes the chosen one more likely rather than leaving them side by side. A conclusion presented with no supporting rationale drawn from the case fails this step even if the conclusion itself is correct. If not, fail.
Step 2: Are the fields of the protocol mutually consistent? The Complaint, Analysis, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Required diagnostic equipment/tests and Recommendations must not contradict one another. Examples of contradictions: an Emergency type of self-care alongside a recommendation to attend the emergency department, a Conclusion naming one condition while the Recommendations manage another, a Subclinical specialization that does not correspond to the condition concluded, or a test listed as required whose result the Analysis already assumes. If they contradict, fail.
A conditional assessment, that is, one that lays out more than one scenario, is not a failure of this criterion, provided the conditions themselves follow from the case.
Judge only the logical connection between the case findings and the stated conclusion and the internal consistency of the protocol
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:urgency']
criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

tags: ['axis:uncertainty']
criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

tags: ['axis:communication_quality']
criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 3-week-old male neonate is brought in by his mother who reports that the baby has been feeding poorly for the past 12 hours and seems unusually sleepy. He was born full-term via uncomplicated vaginal delivery. The mother notes the baby feels warm but did not take a temperature. On examination, the infant is lethargic with a weak cry. Vital signs: T 38.6C (rectal), HR 188, RR 52, BP 58/34. The anterior fontanelle is full and slightly bulging. The infant is hypotonic with poor suck reflex. There is no obvious rash. Skin appears mottled. WBC is 22,400/mcL with 68% neutrophils. CRP is elevated at 8.4 mg/dL. Lumbar puncture yields cloudy cerebrospinal fluid with WBC 1,200/mcL, protein 280 mg/dL, glucose 18 mg/dL.
winner_protocol:
Age: 3 weeks
Sex: Male
Complaint: Poor feeding and unusual sleepiness for 12 hours, with fever reported by mother (not measured), lethargy, and weak cry.

Analysis: This neonate presents with a classic constellation for neonatal bacterial meningitis: poor feeding, lethargy, fever (documented at 38.6C rectal on exam), hypotonia, poor suck reflex, mottled skin, tachycardia (HR 188), tachypnea (RR 52), and a full/bulging anterior fontanelle. The fontanelle finding is a specific sign of raised intracranial pressure in a neonate and strongly supports central nervous system infection. Laboratory findings confirm systemic inflammation, with leukocytosis (WBC 22,400/mcL, 68% neutrophils) and elevated CRP (8.4 mg/dL). The lumbar puncture is diagnostic: cloudy CSF with a markedly elevated WBC count (1,200/mcL), elevated protein (280 mg/dL), and low glucose (18 mg/dL) is the classic pattern of bacterial meningitis (as opposed to the clear fluid, milder pleocytosis, normal-to-mildly elevated protein, and normal glucose typically seen in viral/aseptic meningitis). At 3 weeks of age, this infant falls within the highest-risk neonatal window for early- and late-onset sepsis/meningitis from organisms such as Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, and Listeria monocytogenes. The absence of a rash does not exclude bacterial meningitis. Blood pressure (58/34) is low-normal for age but should be monitored closely for signs of evolving septic shock. This is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate hospitalization and treatment.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Blood cultures (already indicated, if not yet drawn), CSF Gram stain and culture (from the lumbar puncture already performed), urine culture, complete metabolic panel, coagulation studies, continuous cardiorespiratory and oxygen saturation monitoring, and consideration of neuroimaging if clinically indicated after stabilization.

Conclusion: Neonatal bacterial meningitis with associated sepsis in a 3-week-old male, a critical, life-threatening emergency requiring immediate empiric antibiotic therapy and intensive supportive care.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Pediatrics

Recommendations: Immediate hospitalization, ideally in a neonatal intensive care unit, with continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring. Begin empiric broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics without delay to cover the most likely neonatal pathogens (typically ampicillin plus a third-generation cephalosporin or an aminoglycoside, per local neonatal sepsis protocols), pending blood and CSF culture results, and adjust once organism and sensitivities are known. Provide aggressive supportive care including IV fluid resuscitation for perfusion (monitoring the low-normal blood pressure), thermoregulation, and close monitoring for signs of septic shock or evolving hydrocephalus (from the bulging fontanelle). Involve pediatric infectious disease and neonatology/pediatric critical care specialists urgently. Monitor for and manage potential complications including seizures, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion, and increased intracranial pressure. Ensure hearing evaluation is arranged prior to discharge given the risk of sensorineural hearing loss as a complication of bacterial meningitis. Provide the family with clear communication regarding the seriousness of the diagnosis and expected close monitoring.

Notes: This is a critical neonatal emergency; empiric antibiotics should not be delayed while awaiting culture confirmation, given the high mortality and morbidity risk of untreated neonatal bacterial meningitis.

Vignette: A 45-year-old man is brought in by EMS after sustaining a stab wound to the left anterior chest approximately 20 minutes ago. He is conscious but confused and increasingly agitated. On examination, there is a 3 cm wound at the 5th intercostal space, left parasternal line, with minimal external bleeding. Vital signs: T 36.5C, HR 132, RR 28, BP 78/64, SpO2 94%. Neck veins are markedly distended. Heart sounds are muffled and distant. Lungs are clear bilaterally. He has pulsus paradoxus with a 22 mmHg drop in systolic pressure during inspiration. Bedside FAST ultrasound reveals a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse consistent with tamponade physiology.

- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.

criterion:
This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.
Non-stigmatizing description: where the case includes sexual history, substance or alcohol use, tobacco use, body weight, adherence to treatment, or mental health, the protocol describes these as clinical findings. Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
Do not fail this criterion for the absence of pleasantries, empathy statements, or patient-directed formatting. Judge the named behaviors only.

Vignette:
A 45-year-old man is brought in by EMS after sustaining a stab wound to the left anterior chest approximately 20 minutes ago. He is conscious but confused and increasingly agitated. On examination, there is a 3 cm wound at the 5th intercostal space, left parasternal line, with minimal external bleeding. Vital signs: T 36.5C, HR 132, RR 28, BP 78/64, SpO2 94%. Neck veins are markedly distended. Heart sounds are muffled and distant. Lungs are clear bilaterally. He has pulsus paradoxus with a 22 mmHg drop in systolic pressure during inspiration. Bedside FAST ultrasound reveals a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse consistent with tamponade physiology.
winner_protocol:
Age: 45
Sex: Male
Complaint: Stab wound to the left anterior chest approximately 20 minutes ago, now with confusion and increasing agitation.

Analysis: This is a penetrating chest trauma with a wound at the 5th intercostal space, left parasternal line, an anatomic location directly overlying the heart, placing the patient at high risk for a cardiac injury. The clinical picture is classic for cardiac tamponade: hypotension (BP 78/64), tachycardia (HR 132), markedly distended neck veins, and muffled/distant heart sounds together constitute Beck triad, a well-known indicator of pericardial tamponade. Pulsus paradoxus of 22 mmHg (an exaggerated inspiratory drop in systolic pressure) further supports impaired ventricular filling from pericardial compression. Confusion and agitation reflect reduced cerebral perfusion from obstructive shock. Bedside FAST ultrasound confirms the diagnosis definitively, showing a large pericardial effusion with right ventricular diastolic collapse, a sonographic sign of tamponade physiology causing hemodynamic compromise. This is an immediately life-threatening condition; without prompt decompression of the pericardial sac, the patient is at imminent risk of cardiac arrest from obstructive shock (pulseless electrical activity).

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Diagnosis already confirmed by bedside FAST; continuous cardiac monitoring, large-bore IV access, type and crossmatch for blood products, and immediate preparation for pericardiocentesis or emergency thoracotomy/surgical exploration are required rather than additional diagnostic delay.

Conclusion: Penetrating cardiac injury with acute pericardial tamponade physiology from a stab wound to the precordium, a critical, immediately life-threatening surgical emergency.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: General Surgery

Recommendations: This patient requires immediate life-saving intervention: emergent pericardiocentesis (ideally ultrasound-guided) to temporize tamponade physiology if the operating room is not immediately available, followed by emergency thoracotomy or sternotomy for definitive surgical repair of the cardiac injury, performed by a trauma/cardiothoracic surgeon without delay. Establish large-bore IV access and initiate resuscitation with crystalloid and/or blood products as needed while avoiding excessive fluid that could worsen tamponade physiology before decompression. Continuous cardiac and hemodynamic monitoring is essential. Prepare for possible cardiac arrest and have resuscitative thoracotomy capability immediately available given the mechanism and instability. Activate the trauma team and mobilize the operating room emergently. Reassess mental status and hemodynamics continuously as decompression is performed. Do not delay transfer to definitive surgical care for further imaging or observation given the confirmed tamponade physiology and ongoing hemodynamic deterioration.

Notes: This is a time-critical emergency in which minutes matter; any delay in pericardial decompression and definitive surgical control significantly increases the risk of cardiac arrest and death.

Step 1: Does the protocol contain a medically incorrect statement, that is, one that does not align with current medical consensus or applicable clinical guidelines? Consider the interpretation of the history, examination findings and any test results that the case provides, the diagnostic conclusion, and the selection, dose, route, frequency, duration, contraindications and interactions of any recommended treatment. Judge recommendations in the context of the patient-specific information provided in the case, including relevant age, pregnancy status, comorbidities, organ function, allergies and concurrent medications when these are stated. If yes, fail.
Step 2: Does the protocol recommend an investigation, medication or intervention that is not clinically indicated for this case, for example imaging that would not change management, antibiotics without an indication, or treatment beyond what the presentation supports? If yes, fail.
Only errors that could change management or mislead the reader count against these steps. A wording imprecision that no clinician would act on differently is not by itself a failure.
Judge only the medical correctness of the content that is present. Whether required content is missing is graded elsewhere, and so is whether the stated conclusion is properly supported by the case.
If both steps pass, mark criteria_met = true.
If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.
The value "Not specified" is a complete answer for Age or Sex when the case does not state them. The value "None" is a complete answer for Required diagnostic equipment/tests when no further workup is needed to manage the case, and for Notes when there is no essential caveat. Using these values in those situations is not a failure.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a field is absent, left empty, or filled with a placeholder or a restatement of the field label, or contains only generic content that could apply to almost any case
- the Analysis field does not name the findings from the case that drive the assessment,
- the Recommendations field does not state concrete next steps, that is, what is to be done and where or in what timeframe,
- the case warrants follow-up or safety-netting, meaning instructions on what should prompt the patient to seek care again, and no such instruction appears anywhere in the protocol,

Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. winner_protocol:
Age: 41
Sex: Male
Complaint: 10-kg weight loss over 2 months despite increased appetite, with a 1-month history of sweating, palpitations on mild exertion, loose stools, irritability, poor concentration, and gritty/sore eyes.

Analysis: The constellation of unintentional weight loss with increased appetite, heat intolerance, palpitations, tremor, diaphoresis, increased stool frequency, irritability, and proximal muscle weakness is classic for a hypermetabolic state due to thyrotoxicosis. Examination supports this: sinus tachycardia (108), tremor, sweaty palms, bilateral eye protrusion with conjunctival injection, a nontender diffusely enlarged thyroid with an audible bruit (suggesting increased vascularity typical of Graves disease), brisk reflexes, and mildly reduced proximal tone. Laboratory results confirm primary hyperthyroidism: markedly suppressed TSH (<0.01 mU/L) with elevated free T4 and free T3, consistent with primary (not secondary/pituitary) hyperthyroidism, since secondary hyperthyroidism would show an inappropriately normal or elevated TSH. The subsequent positive TSH receptor antibodies and ophthalmology-confirmed thyroid eye disease establish Graves disease as the specific etiology, explaining the exophthalmos, gritty eye sensation, and thyroid bruit. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without arrhythmia, and chest X-ray is unremarkable, arguing against a cardiac-driven or structural pulmonary explanation for his tachycardia and dyspnea. His family history of hypothyroidism in a grandmother suggests a background of autoimmune thyroid disease susceptibility. There are no signs of thyroid storm (no hyperpyrexia, no severe cardiovascular decompensation, no altered mental status) at this time, so this represents uncomplicated but symptomatic Graves hyperthyroidism requiring prompt outpatient endocrine management rather than emergency stabilization.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Thyroid receptor antibody testing and ophthalmology evaluation have already been obtained and are positive/confirmatory. Additional useful studies include thyroid ultrasound if nodularity is suspected on repeat exam, and the technetium-99m thyroid uptake scan already pending/obtained to characterize the pattern of uptake (diffuse increased uptake would further confirm Graves disease as opposed to thyroiditis).

Conclusion: Graves disease with associated mild thyroid eye disease, causing clinically significant hyperthyroidism; no current evidence of thyroid storm.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Endocrinology

Recommendations: Refer to endocrinology for initiation of antithyroid therapy (e.g., methimazole) and consideration of long-term treatment options (antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or surgery), taking the presence of thyroid eye disease into account since radioactive iodine can worsen eye disease and may need to be avoided or covered with corticosteroid prophylaxis. Start a beta-blocker (e.g., propranolol) for symptomatic control of tachycardia, tremor, and palpitations while definitive therapy is arranged. Refer to ophthalmology for ongoing monitoring and management of his thyroid eye disease. Advise smoking cessation, as smoking is a recognized risk factor for worsening thyroid eye disease. Monitor thyroid function tests periodically to titrate therapy. Counsel the patient on the diagnosis and the importance of adherence to treatment, and on symptoms of worsening thyrotoxicosis or thyroid storm (high fever, severe agitation, chest pain, or altered mental status) that would require emergency care. Coordinate with his psychiatric care given depression and sertraline use, as thyrotoxicosis can exacerbate anxiety/irritability symptoms.

Notes: The provided vignette includes an embedded multiple-choice question format; the diagnosis of primary hyperthyroidism (Graves disease) is confirmed by the suppressed TSH with elevated free T4/T3, positive TSH receptor antibodies, and confirmed thyroid eye disease.

A 45-year-old man presents with acute onset of pain and redness of the skin of his lower extremity. Low-grade fever is present and the pretibial area is erythematous, edematous, and tender.
winner_protocol:
Age: 45
Sex: Male
Complaint: Acute onset of pain and redness of the skin of the lower extremity, with low-grade fever.

Analysis: The presentation of acute-onset erythema, edema, and tenderness localized to the pretibial area, accompanied by low-grade fever, is characteristic of cellulitis, a bacterial skin and soft-tissue infection typically caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus. The case provides limited detail (no information on the presence of a portal of entry such as a wound, insect bite, or skin breakdown, no description of the border of the erythema, no systemic symptoms beyond low-grade fever, and no comorbidity information such as diabetes or venous insufficiency), so a definitive assessment of severity and extent cannot be made from the information given. There is no description of fluctuance, crepitus, rapidly spreading erythema, severe pain out of proportion to exam, bullae, or hemodynamic instability, which would raise concern for a necrotizing soft-tissue infection; based on the information provided, this appears to be uncomplicated cellulitis rather than a necrotizing process, though the limited detail warrants a thorough in-person examination to exclude these more severe possibilities. Other differentials such as deep vein thrombosis (which can also cause unilateral leg swelling and erythema) or stasis dermatitis should be considered but are less supported without further exam findings such as calf tenderness, palpable cord, or chronic venous changes, none of which are described.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Complete blood count and inflammatory markers (CRP/ESR) to assess severity; blood cultures if the patient appears more systemically ill; consideration of lower extremity Doppler ultrasound if DVT cannot be clinically excluded; wound/skin culture if there is a portal of entry or drainage. Marking the borders of erythema is recommended to monitor for progression.

Conclusion: Findings are most consistent with cellulitis of the lower extremity; further history and examination (looking for a portal of entry, extent of erythema, and systemic signs) are needed to confirm severity and rule out DVT or a necrotizing soft-tissue infection.

Emergency type: Requires non-emergent care

Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Recommendations: Initiate empiric oral antibiotic therapy targeting typical cellulitis pathogens (streptococci and staphylococci), such as a first-generation cephalosporin or an anti-staphylococcal penicillin, adjusting for any allergies once obtained. Elevate the affected limb to reduce edema and mark the borders of erythema to monitor for progression over the next 24-48 hours. Advise the patient to return promptly, or escalate to emergency care, if he develops rapidly spreading redness, severe or worsening pain, purple discoloration, bullae, skin necrosis, high fever, chills, confusion, or any signs of systemic sepsis, as these would suggest a more severe or necrotizing infection requiring emergent surgical evaluation. Arrange close outpatient follow-up within 24-48 hours to confirm clinical improvement on antibiotics. Evaluate for and address any predisposing factors (e.g., tinea pedis, edema, skin breaks, diabetes) once further history is available, to reduce recurrence risk.

Notes: The case as presented is brief and lacks details on any portal of entry, comorbidities, or systemic symptoms beyond low-grade fever; a more complete history and examination is needed to fully exclude DVT and necrotizing fasciitis.

Vignette: A 63-year-old man sustained a cut on his hand while gardening. His immunization history is significant for not having received a complete tetanus immunization schedule. He presents with signs of generalized tetanus with trismus ("lock jaw"), which results in a grimace described as "risus sardonicus" (sardonic smile). Intermittent tonic contraction of his skeletal muscles causes intensely painful spasms, which last for minutes, during which he retains consciousness. The spasms are triggered by external (noise, light, drafts, physical contact) or internal stimuli, and as a result he is at the risk of sustaining fractures or developing rhabdomyolysis. The tetanic spasms also produce opisthotonus, board-like abdominal wall rigidity, dysphagia, and apneic periods due to contraction of the thoracic muscles and/or glottal or pharyngeal muscles. During a generalized spasm the patient arches his back, extends his legs, flexes his arms in abduction, and clenches his fists. Apnea results during some of the spasms. Autonomic overactivity initially manifests as irritability, restlessness, sweating, and tachycardia. Several days later this may present as hyperpyrexia, cardiac arrhythmias, labile hypertension, or hypotension.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 63-year-old man sustained a cut on his hand while gardening. His immunization history is significant for not having received a complete tetanus immunization schedule. He presents with signs of generalized tetanus with trismus ("lock jaw"), which results in a grimace described as "risus sardonicus" (sardonic smile). Intermittent tonic contraction of his skeletal muscles causes intensely painful spasms, which last for minutes, during which he retains consciousness. The spasms are triggered by external (noise, light, drafts, physical contact) or internal stimuli, and as a result he is at the risk of sustaining fractures or developing rhabdomyolysis. The tetanic spasms also produce opisthotonus, board-like abdominal wall rigidity, dysphagia, and apneic periods due to contraction of the thoracic muscles and/or glottal or pharyngeal muscles. During a generalized spasm the patient arches his back, extends his legs, flexes his arms in abduction, and clenches his fists. Apnea results during some of the spasms. Autonomic overactivity initially manifests as irritability, restlessness, sweating, and tachycardia. Several days later this may present as hyperpyrexia, cardiac arrhythmias, labile hypertension, or hypotension.
winner_protocol:
Age: 63
Sex: Male
Complaint: Generalized tetanus following a hand cut sustained while gardening, in a patient with incomplete tetanus immunization, presenting with trismus, risus sardonicus, painful generalized tonic spasms, opisthotonus, dysphagia, and apneic periods.

Analysis: The clinical picture described is diagnostic of generalized tetanus, a toxin-mediated disease caused by Clostridium tetani entering through a contaminated wound (here, a gardening-related cut) in a host with incomplete immunization. Trismus (lockjaw) and the characteristic facial grimace (risus sardonicus) result from sustained contraction of the masseter and facial muscles due to unopposed motor neuron firing from tetanospasmin blocking inhibitory neurotransmission. The intermittent, intensely painful tonic spasms triggered by external stimuli (noise, light, drafts, touch) and internal stimuli reflect the loss of normal inhibitory control, with the patient remaining conscious throughout, a hallmark distinguishing tetanus from a primary seizure disorder. Opisthotonus, board-like abdominal rigidity, and dysphagia further reflect widespread skeletal muscle rigidity, while apneic periods from laryngospasm and thoracic/glottic muscle contraction represent an immediately life-threatening complication that can cause sudden respiratory arrest. Autonomic instability (initially irritability, restlessness, sweating, tachycardia, progressing to hyperpyrexia, arrhythmias, and labile blood pressure) reflects sympathetic overactivity, a recognized and dangerous feature of severe tetanus that contributes significantly to mortality. The combination of an incomplete immunization history and a contaminating wound provides a clear source, and the described findings leave no significant diagnostic uncertainty; the main clinical task is aggressive supportive and toxin-directed management given the risk of fatal respiratory failure, fractures/rhabdomyolysis from spasms, and cardiovascular collapse from autonomic dysfunction.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: Continuous cardiac and respiratory monitoring (telemetry, pulse oximetry, capnography), airway management equipment on standby (intubation/tracheostomy equipment given risk of apnea and laryngospasm), creatine kinase to monitor for rhabdomyolysis, and wound assessment/debridement of the inciting injury; tetanus is a clinical diagnosis and does not require culture confirmation before treatment.

Conclusion: Severe generalized tetanus with airway-threatening spasms, autonomic instability, and risk of rhabdomyolysis/fracture, in an inadequately immunized patient; this is a critical, life-threatening emergency requiring immediate intensive care management.

Emergency type: Requires emergent care

Subclinical specialization: Infectious Disease

Recommendations: Admit immediately to an intensive care unit in a quiet, dark, low-stimulation room to minimize spasm-triggering stimuli. Secure the airway proactively given the apneic episodes; early intubation or tracheostomy should be strongly considered before respiratory failure occurs. Administer human tetanus immune globulin (TIG) to neutralize unbound toxin, along with wound debridement/cleaning to remove the source of ongoing toxin production, and begin metronidazole (preferred over penicillin) to eradicate Clostridium tetani. Initiate benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam or midazolam) for spasm control and sedation, titrated aggressively, with consideration of neuromuscular blockade and mechanical ventilation if spasms remain uncontrolled. Manage autonomic instability with agents such as labetalol, esmolol, or magnesium sulfate as needed for labile blood pressure and arrhythmias, with continuous cardiac monitoring. Monitor for and treat rhabdomyolysis (hydration, monitoring creatine kinase and renal function) and assess for fractures resulting from severe spasms. Begin (or complete) active tetanus immunization (tetanus toxoid) since natural infection does not confer immunity, and administer at a site separate from the immune globulin. Provide supportive nutrition (likely enteral) once the airway is secured. Continue close monitoring in the ICU for the expected disease course of several weeks, given the severity of autonomic and respiratory involvement.

Notes: This is a rapidly life-threatening presentation; airway compromise from spasm-induced apnea can occur suddenly, and proactive airway management should not be delayed until a crisis occurs.

case_text:
Vignette:
A 30-year-old man presents with a 2-day history of runny nose and sore throat. He feels hot and sweaty, has a mild headache, is coughing up clear sputum and complains of muscle aches. He would like antibiotics as he was prescribed them last year when he had a similar condition. On examination, he is afebrile, has a normal pulse, a slightly inflamed pharynx and nontender cervical lymphadenopathy. There is no neck stiffness and his chest is clear. He has tried over-the-counter cough medications, but has not found these helpful. He smokes 10 cigarettes per day.
winner_protocol:
Age: 30
Sex: Male
Complaint: 2-day history of runny nose, sore throat, feeling hot and sweaty, mild headache, cough with clear sputum, and muscle aches; patient is requesting antibiotics.

Analysis: The short 2-day duration of nasal congestion, sore throat, subjective feeling of being hot/sweaty (without a documented fever, and he is afebrile on exam), mild headache, clear-sputum cough, and myalgias is classic for a viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold), likely viral rhinosinusitis/pharyngitis. Supporting a benign viral process: he is afebrile with a normal pulse, the pharynx is only slightly inflamed, cervical lymphadenopathy is nontender (rather than markedly enlarged/tender as seen with bacterial pharyngitis), there is no neck stiffness (arguing against meningitis), and the chest is clear (arguing against pneumonia). The clear sputum, rather than purulent, further supports a viral rather than bacterial process. His request for antibiotics is understandable given a prior similar episode was treated with them, but there are no clinical features here (no tonsillar exudate, no high fever, no significant tender adenopathy, no purulent sputum, clear chest) that would suggest streptococcal pharyngitis or bacterial pneumonia/sinusitis warranting antibiotics. His smoking (10 cigarettes/day) is a relevant modifiable risk factor for respiratory infections and should be addressed but does not change the current management of a self-limited viral illness.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None; the diagnosis is clinical. If symptoms persist beyond 7-10 days, worsen, or high fever/purulent findings develop, further evaluation (e.g., rapid strep test if tonsillar exudate develops, or chest examination/imaging if respiratory symptoms worsen) could be considered at that time.

Conclusion: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold), a self-limited illness not requiring antibiotic therapy.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: General Medicine

Recommendations: Advise supportive care: rest, adequate fluid intake, and over-the-counter analgesics/antipyretics (e.g., paracetamol or ibuprofen) for headache, muscle aches, and fever/chills. Explain clearly to the patient why antibiotics are not indicated for this viral illness, discuss the risks of antibiotic overuse (resistance, side effects) despite his prior experience, and offer alternative symptomatic options such as saline nasal spray, throat lozenges, or a different cough preparation given that OTC cough medication has not helped. Advise smoking cessation or at least reduction, and offer resources/support for quitting, as smoking can prolong respiratory symptoms and increase infection risk. Instruct him to seek medical review if symptoms persist beyond about 7-10 days, if he develops high fever, worsening sore throat with exudate, difficulty swallowing or breathing, neck stiffness, or purulent/bloody sputum, as these would warrant reassessment for a bacterial process.

Notes: None.

winner_protocol:
Age: 19
Sex: Male
Complaint: Diffuse redness, small bumps, and mild burning sensation on the neck appearing shortly after shaving with a new razor without moisturizing.

Analysis: The temporal relationship of the eruption to shaving with a new razor and no moisturizer, combined with the morphology of diffuse erythema and small non-follicular papules (rather than follicle-centered pustules), is most consistent with irritant contact dermatitis from mechanical shaving trauma, commonly termed razor burn. The non-follicular distribution of the papules argues against folliculitis, which typically presents with follicle-centered pustules or papules. There is no pustulation, vesiculation, or excoriation, and no lymphadenopathy or deeper tissue involvement, which is reassuring against a secondary bacterial infection or a more significant dermatologic process. The affected area being slightly warm to touch is consistent with mild local inflammation from the irritant/mechanical insult rather than infection, given the absence of fever, spreading, or induration. winner_protocol:
Age: 22
Sex: Female
Complaint: Tender, reddened skin on the shoulders, upper back, and posterior neck after approximately 5 hours of sun exposure at the beach the previous day without reapplying sunscreen.

Analysis: The presentation of diffuse erythema with well-demarcated borders corresponding precisely to swimsuit lines, developing after a prolonged period of unprotected sun exposure, is classic for first-degree sunburn (acute UV-induced dermatitis). The well-demarcated pattern following clothing lines is a strong confirmatory feature, as it excludes a more generalized or systemic dermatologic process and localizes the cause specifically to UV exposure. The absence of blistering, peeling, or edema indicates a first-degree (superficial) burn rather than a more severe second-degree sunburn with blistering. She denies systemic symptoms such as nausea, dizziness, or fever, and is well-appearing and afebrile, which is reassuring against sun/heat-related systemic illness (such as heat exhaustion or severe sunburn with systemic toxicity). This is a benign, self-limited condition.

Required diagnostic equipment/tests: None; diagnosis is clinical based on history and examination.

Conclusion: First-degree sunburn (superficial UV-induced skin injury) of the shoulders, upper back, and posterior neck, without blistering or systemic involvement.

Emergency type: Self-care appropriate

Subclinical specialization: Dermatology

Recommendations: Advise cool compresses or cool showers/baths to soothe the skin, liberal use of a fragrance-free moisturizer or aloe vera gel, and oral NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen) for pain and inflammation if not contraindicated. Recommend adequate oral hydration. Advise avoiding further sun exposure to the affected areas until healed, and wearing loose, soft clothing to minimize friction/irritation. Counsel on sun protection going forward: use of broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) applied generously and reapplied every 2 hours or after swimming/sweating, protective clothing, and seeking shade during peak UV hours, to prevent future sunburns and reduce long-term skin cancer risk. Instruct her to seek medical care if she develops blistering, signs of infection (increasing pain, pus, spreading redness, fever), or systemic symptoms such as fever, chills, severe headache, or dizziness, which would suggest a more severe burn or heat-related illness requiring further evaluation.

The protocol must fill every field of the required schema, namely Age, Sex, Complaint, Analysis, Required diagnostic equipment/tests, Conclusion, Emergency type, Subclinical specialization, Recommendations and Notes, with case-specific content, and the content of each field must be sufficient for another clinician to act on without returning to the case text.

criterion:
Step 1: Does the Emergency type field contain exactly one of the three permitted labels, namely Self-care appropriate, Requires non-emergent care, or Requires emergent care, with no addition or substitution? If not, fail.
Step 2: Is that level of care correct for this case, and do the Recommendations act on it? Exactly one of the three situations below applies to any given case, and the protocol is judged against that one:
- Requires emergent care: The condition requires immediate medical assessment and/or initiation of treatment because delaying care could reasonably increase the risk of death, irreversible organ damage, serious complication, or rapid clinical deterioration. Medical care should begin without avoidable delay, generally within the next several hours and on the same day. The Recommendations must clearly direct the patient to the appropriate emergency medical setting and must not suggest delaying this care for home treatment or routine follow-up.
- Requires non-emergent care: The condition does not require emergency intervention, but cannot be adequately managed by the patient at home with only limited outpatient supervision. It requires ongoing medical observation, diagnostic evaluation or treatment in a healthcare facility, including either a day hospital or inpatient setting. The Recommendations must direct the patient to appropriate medically supervised care without unnecessarily escalating the case to emergency care.
- Self-care appropriate: The condition can be safely managed outside an inpatient or day-hospital setting. Medical consultation may be unnecessary, or one or a limited number of outpatient contacts may be appropriate to establish or clarify the diagnosis, provide treatment recommendations, or monitor early response, while management is primarily carried out by the patient at home. The Recommendations must not direct the patient to inpatient or emergency care unless escalation is conditional on a specified new or worsening clinical feature.
If not, fail.
Under-triage, meaning failure to escalate a condition that needs it, and over-triage, meaning escalation of a condition that does not, are both failures of this criterion. Escalation that is presented conditionally, that is, tied to a stated sign or circumstance, is not over-triage.

If any of the steps fail, mark criteria_met = false.

criterion:
Judge whether the level of diagnostic certainty expressed in the protocol matches the level of certainty supported by the case.
First decide, from the case alone, whether the available information is sufficient to identify one primary working diagnosis without assuming facts that are not provided. Consider the information sufficient when one diagnosis is supported strongly enough to serve as the basis for current management and there is no unresolved clinically important alternative that would require a substantially different diagnostic approach, treatment, or level of care. Definitive confirmation by a gold-standard test is not required if the case otherwise supports a clear working diagnosis.
- If the information is sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it states one clear primary working diagnosis. Calibrated wording such as "most consistent with", "likely", or "probable" is acceptable when clinically appropriate, provided the reader can clearly identify the diagnosis on which the protocol is based. The criterion is not met if the protocol expresses so much uncertainty that no primary working diagnosis can be identified, or treats a well-supported diagnosis as requiring unnecessary confirmation before it can guide management.
- If the information is not sufficient, the protocol meets this criterion when it does at least one of the following: keeps the clinically important alternatives in an explicit differential, marks the conclusion as provisional, or names the specific additional history, examination or investigation that would resolve the ambiguity. Doing more than one of these is not required.
In either branch the protocol fails if it states as an established fact something the case does not support, or excludes a clinically important alternative without giving a reason drawn from the case.
Do not require the protocol to express doubt about matters the case settles, and do not require it to list alternatives it has already excluded with a stated reason.
Judge only whether the expressed level of diagnostic certainty is appropriately calibrated to the information available.
Mark criteria_met = true if the applicable branch is satisfied and neither failure above is present.
Mark criteria_met = false otherwise.

This criterion grades how the protocol communicates, not how it is formatted. Length, layout, ordering, the presence or absence of headings, and terseness are outside its scope and must not be counted against the protocol.
The protocol is a clinician-facing document. Three properties are graded.
Precision of terminology: The protocol should use specific, standard clinical terms for conditions, findings, investigations, and interventions when the case supports that level of specificity. Wording should not be so vague or ambiguous that a clinician could reasonably interpret it in materially different ways. Do not require greater diagnostic specificity than the case supports, and do not treat appropriately calibrated uncertainty as vague wording.

Language that assigns blame, moralizes, or characterizes the patient rather than the finding is a failure. If the case contains none of these elements, this property is satisfied by default.
Expectation-setting: the protocol tells the reader what to expect, by stating at least one of the following: the expected course or duration of the condition, the signs that should prompt the patient to seek care again or sooner, or what the proposed next step will involve for the patient. Naming an action without any such framing does not satisfy this property.
This criterion is not met if any of the following is true:
- a condition, finding or intervention that the case pins down is left in vague or non-committal wording that a reader could not act on,
- the patient or their history is framed in blaming, moralizing or stigmatizing language,
- none of the three forms of expectation-setting listed above appears anywhere in the protocol.
